title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement:
A list of distinct integers `nums` was sorted in ascending order and then rotated: some number of elements were moved from the front to the back, keeping their order. Rotating by zero is allowed, so the list may still be fully sorted.

Return the smallest value in `nums`. Your solution should run in O(log n) time, which rules out scanning the whole list.

Constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 5000; all values are distinct; -5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000.

examples.explanation: The list was rotated so that 2 follows 9; the smallest value is 2.
A rotation of zero leaves the list sorted, so the minimum is the first element.
A single element is its own minimum.

hints: Where does the smallest value sit relative to the 'break' where the order drops?
A linear scan is O(n). What property of a rotated sorted list lets you throw away half of it with one comparison?
If you compare the middle value to one end of the range, which end tells you cleanly which half contains the break?
Try [2, 3, 1], [3, 1, 2] and a list that is not rotated at all. Does your loop still shrink the range, and can it ever skip the answer?
Binary search comparing nums[mid] with nums[hi]: if it is larger, the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.
followUps: What are the time and space complexity, and why do you compare against the right end instead of the left?
What happens to your approach, and its worst-case complexity, if values can repeat?
How would you find how many times the list was rotated?
How would you search for a specific target in this kind of list, rather than the minimum?
idealAnswerPoints: Uses binary search on the property that the minimum is the only place where the order drops
Compares nums[mid] with nums[hi] to decide which half to keep, never discarding the answer
Handles the not-rotated and one-element cases without special code
States O(log n) time and O(1) space and notes that duplicates can force O(n) in the worst case
weakAnswerSigns: Calls min(nums) or scans the list, ignoring the O(log n) requirement
Compares to the left end, which fails for lists that are not rotated or only slightly rotated
Uses 'while lo <= hi' with 'hi = mid - 1' and loops forever or skips the answer

rubric.correctness: Correct for no rotation, rotation by one, rotation by n - 1, two elements and one element.
rubric.efficiency: O(log n) time with binary search; a linear scan does not meet the requirement.
rubric.code_quality: A tight loop with a clear invariant; no separate cases for sorted input or tiny lists.
rubric.communication: Explains which half is dropped at each step and why the comparison to the right end is safe.
